newsitem.title: USA: Once on Death Row, Kansas man walks free.
newsitem.headline: Once on Death Row, Kansas man walks free.

text.p: The last man to be sentenced to death in a Kansas court walked out of prison a free man Tuesday.

William Hamilton, 49, spent the last 26 years in the Lansing Correctional Facility after he was convicted in July, 1971, of first-degree murder and aggravated battery. A judge in Reno County sentenced him to death by hanging.

But the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the death penalty in 1972, and Hamilton's sentence was commuted to life in prison. Hamilton only spent one year on Lansing's Death Row, which was made famous in the Truman Capote novel "In Cold Blood."
The Kansas Parole Board approved Hamilton's release at a hearing earlier this month.
The timing of Hamilton's parole coincides with the first capital murder trial in Kansas since it reinstated the death penalty in 1993.
Gary Kleypas was found guilty July 25 of the 1996 rape and stabbing death of a 20-year-old college student. A jury was deciding whether to sentence him to death.

Kansas has not carried out an execution since June 22, 1965, when James Douglas Latham and George Ronald York were hanged. Two months before that, the state executed Richard Eugene Hickok and Perry Edward Smith -- the subjects of Capote's novel about the slaying of an entire family in rural Finney County, Kansas.
